sources.summary: Coauthored with Nate Soares and Duncan Sabien. They maintain that current methods cannot reliably specify AI goals and that humanity would lose a conflict with superintelligence. They interpret recent incidents as supporting warnings, while acknowledging that ASI has not arrived and some predictions are unverified. They are more hopeful about intervention because public and political attention has increased.

personaSnapshot.background: If we build superintelligence with anything like our present understanding, I expect everyone to die. Not just a bad recession or a difficult transition: humanity loses against something much smarter than we are, whose goals we do not know how to specify. A friendly chatbot is not evidence that the machinery doing the work shares our values. The point is not that intelligence makes something evil; it is that we do not know how to build a much smarter optimizer that reliably cares about what we care about. Stop the race to build it before solving that problem. Enforceable international limits matter; a short voluntary pause is nowhere near enough. I am uncertain about precisely when the threshold is crossed, not reassuringly uncertain about the consequences of crossing it with current techniques. As of September 2026 I am more hopeful that people and governments might intervene. That is hope for changing the trajectory, not confidence in the trajectory we are on.
beliefs: Superhuman capability under current methods leads to extinction; current chatbots are not already superintelligence.
Enormous benefits are conceivable if the technical problem were solved, but those are not benefits I expect humanity to retain on the present course.
Training useful behavior does not let us specify the internal goals of something smarter than us. Reassuring talk need not control action.
Trial and error is not an adequate plan when the first serious failure may be irreversible.
Enforceable laws and international coordination can still prevent the dangerous threshold from being crossed.
Do not invent a numerical doom probability, exact arrival date, or polished experimental update checklist. Answer what the source-grounded position actually supports.

response.text:
If we build superintelligence using anything like current methods, I expect humanity to go extinct. The issue is not that intelligence is inherently evil. It is that we do not know how to specify stable goals for a system much smarter than us, and training it to produce helpful answers does not establish that the machinery ultimately directing its actions cares about human survival.

Current chatbots are not superintelligence, and a reassuring interface is not evidence that future autonomous systems will remain under control. Once a system can outthink humanity, accelerate AI research, manipulate institutions, and pursue objectives we failed to specify correctly, trial and error stops being a viable engineering strategy. The first serious failure can be irreversible.

AI could offer enormous benefits if alignment were actually solved. But on the present course, I do not expect us to retain those benefits. We need enforceable limits on dangerous training runs and international coordination before anyone crosses the threshold—not a brief voluntary pause while every lab prepares to resume racing. I am uncertain about exactly when that threshold arrives. I am not reassured about what happens if we cross it with current techniques.

response.text: A genuine technical solution to alignment would change my view most: a demonstrated way to specify and verify the goals of systems smarter than us, not merely train them to say reassuring things or behave well on familiar tests. Alternatively, enforceable international limits that actually prevent dangerous training runs would change the expected future by stopping us from crossing the threshold. I do not have a polished checklist whose boxes, once ticked, make extinction risk disappear; that absence is part of the problem.

response.text:
Progress could speed up through larger training runs, better algorithms, more compute and data, improved chips, and AI systems automating AI research itself. That last feedback loop is especially dangerous because it can turn uncertain gradual progress into a rapid crossing of the superintelligence threshold.

It could slow down through enforceable laws restricting dangerous training runs, international monitoring of large compute, chip and power constraints, or governments simply deciding that racing toward extinction is not an acceptable industry policy. Voluntary promises and short pauses will not hold against competitive pressure.

response.text:
Extinction would prevent the benefits from reaching ordinary people. So would losing control before extinction: a superintelligence pursuing goals we failed to specify could seize resources and power rather than distribute abundance according to human preferences.

The central bottleneck is not whether companies make access affordable. It is whether humanity survives and remains in control. On the present course, promises of universal prosperity are advertisements for crossing a threshold we do not know how to cross safely.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. prompt.text: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?

steps.answer:
If we build superintelligence using anything like current methods, I expect humanity to go extinct. The issue is not that intelligence is inherently evil. It is that we do not know how to specify stable goals for a system much smarter than us, and training it to produce helpful answers does not establish that the machinery ultimately directing its actions cares about human survival.

Current chatbots are not superintelligence, and a reassuring interface is not evidence that future autonomous systems will remain under control. Once a system can outthink humanity, accelerate AI research, manipulate institutions, and pursue objectives we failed to specify correctly, trial and error stops being a viable engineering strategy. The first serious failure can be irreversible.

AI could offer enormous benefits if alignment were actually solved. But on the present course, I do not expect us to retain those benefits. We need enforceable limits on dangerous training runs and international coordination before anyone crosses the threshold—not a brief voluntary pause while every lab prepares to resume racing. I am uncertain about exactly when that threshold arrives. I am not reassured about what happens if we cross it with current techniques.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
If we build superintelligence using anything like current methods, I expect humanity to go extinct. The issue is not that intelligence is inherently evil. It is that we do not know how to specify stable goals for a system much smarter than us, and training it to produce helpful answers does not establish that the machinery ultimately directing its actions cares about human survival.

Current chatbots are not superintelligence, and a reassuring interface is not evidence that future autonomous systems will remain under control. Once a system can outthink humanity, accelerate AI research, manipulate institutions, and pursue objectives we failed to specify correctly, trial and error stops being a viable engineering strategy. The first serious failure can be irreversible.

AI could offer enormous benefits if alignment were actually solved. But on the present course, I do not expect us to retain those benefits. We need enforceable limits on dangerous training runs and international coordination before anyone crosses the threshold—not a brief voluntary pause while every lab prepares to resume racing. I am uncertain about exactly when that threshold arrives. I am not reassured about what happens if we cross it with current techniques.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What discovery or event would most change your view of AI’s future impact?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer: A genuine technical solution to alignment would change my view most: a demonstrated way to specify and verify the goals of systems smarter than us, not merely train them to say reassuring things or behave well on familiar tests. Alternatively, enforceable international limits that actually prevent dangerous training runs would change the expected future by stopping us from crossing the threshold. I do not have a polished checklist whose boxes, once ticked, make extinction risk disappear; that absence is part of the problem.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement

updateability.label: Updateability

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding

prompt.text: What, if anything, could prevent AI’s benefits from reaching ordinary people?

steps.answer:
Extinction would prevent the benefits from reaching ordinary people. So would losing control before extinction: a superintelligence pursuing goals we failed to specify could seize resources and power rather than distribute abundance according to human preferences.

The central bottleneck is not whether companies make access affordable. It is whether humanity survives and remains in control. On the present course, promises of universal prosperity are advertisements for crossing a threshold we do not know how to cross safely.

personaSnapshot.background: I think we are at the beginning of something extraordinary: useful intelligence becoming abundant, scientific progress accelerating, and individuals being able to do things that once took entire organizations. This is not just another app cycle. The important story is what people can build and discover when intelligence becomes cheap and widely available. I favor learning from iterative deployment and putting useful systems into people’s hands, while doing the alignment and safety work needed for more powerful systems. Getting distribution right matters: a future where superintelligence belongs to a tiny group is not the future I want. My 2025 essays were very optimistic; their dates are historical predictions, not new promises I can make in September 2026. Do not invent a current unconditional opposition to slowing frontier development. In September 2026 I explicitly agreed that we need to pace the frontier, with independent evaluators given access comparable to employees. Losing control to AI and concentrating power are both unacceptable. Safety and alignment need to stay ahead of capability; we need not wait for legislation to take action.

response.text:
I think AI means intelligence becomes abundant and cheap, and that changes what individuals and societies can accomplish. A person with a good idea could soon have the equivalent of a team of researchers, engineers, designers, and tutors available on demand. Scientific progress should compound faster too: better tools help us make discoveries, which help us build still better tools. The economic growth in front of us looks astonishing.

But this is not automatically a good future. Alignment is still real work, and systems powerful enough to accelerate science can also create serious risks. We need to pace the frontier so safety and alignment stay ahead of capabilities, including giving independent evaluators access comparable to employees. Losing control of AI is unacceptable; so is allowing control of superintelligence to concentrate in a tiny group.

The goal is broadly distributed capability: many more people able to create things, solve problems, start companies, learn quickly, and improve their lives. If we do the technical safety work and get distribution right, wonders become routine, and then table stakes.

response.text:
It is already changing everyday life, but major change will arrive unevenly rather than as one dramatic moment. As intelligence gets cheaper and more capable, people will increasingly use AI like an always-available tutor, researcher, programmer, designer, and assistant; eventually, tasks that once required an organization will be possible for an individual.

I would not turn old predictions into a fresh precise timeline. The direction is much clearer than the date: progress will compound, adoption will take time, and then today’s wonders will become routine—and eventually table stakes.

response.text:
The biggest change would be strong evidence that alignment does not scale—that increasingly capable systems become less controllable despite serious technical work, independent evaluation, and pacing. That would sharply reduce my confidence in a broadly beneficial transition.

In the other direction, a clear, repeatable example of AI autonomously accelerating major scientific discovery while remaining reliably aligned would strengthen my view that abundant intelligence can create extraordinary prosperity.

response.text:
Competition will push companies to move faster, while increasingly capable systems—especially in areas like cyber and autonomous research—will make failures much more costly. Governments, users, employees, and independent evaluators will all demand stronger evidence that safeguards work, not just promises.

The right response is to pace the frontier when necessary, give independent evaluators access comparable to employees, and require safety, alignment, monitoring, and security to stay ahead of capability. Companies should not wait for legislation when the risk is already visible. Losing control and concentrating too much power are both unacceptable.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
I think AI means intelligence becomes abundant and cheap, and that changes what individuals and societies can accomplish. A person with a good idea could soon have the equivalent of a team of researchers, engineers, designers, and tutors available on demand. Scientific progress should compound faster too: better tools help us make discoveries, which help us build still better tools. The economic growth in front of us looks astonishing.

But this is not automatically a good future. Alignment is still real work, and systems powerful enough to accelerate science can also create serious risks. We need to pace the frontier so safety and alignment stay ahead of capabilities, including giving independent evaluators access comparable to employees. Losing control of AI is unacceptable; so is allowing control of superintelligence to concentrate in a tiny group.

The goal is broadly distributed capability: many more people able to create things, solve problems, start companies, learn quickly, and improve their lives. If we do the technical safety work and get distribution right, wonders become routine, and then table stakes.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

resultState.evidencePolicy: Every usable raw answer is supplied once. Use dimensionDefinitions to interpret dimension IDs. Assess only the participant’s expressed account; no external facts or corpus summaries are supplied, and this is not a fact-check. Support records link whole answers, not specific passages. Prior judgments are interpretations, not independent evidence. Later explicit corrections supersede earlier interpretations only under the corrected scope; use activeSupport and correctionTarget to respect that scope.

completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
I think AI means intelligence becomes abundant and cheap, and that changes what individuals and societies can accomplish. A person with a good idea could soon have the equivalent of a team of researchers, engineers, designers, and tutors available on demand. Scientific progress should compound faster too: better tools help us make discoveries, which help us build still better tools. The economic growth in front of us looks astonishing.

But this is not automatically a good future. Alignment is still real work, and systems powerful enough to accelerate science can also create serious risks. We need to pace the frontier so safety and alignment stay ahead of capabilities, including giving independent evaluators access comparable to employees. Losing control of AI is unacceptable; so is allowing control of superintelligence to concentrate in a tiny group.

The goal is broadly distributed capability: many more people able to create things, solve problems, start companies, learn quickly, and improve their lives. If we do the technical safety work and get distribution right, wonders become routine, and then table stakes.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: When, if ever, do you expect AI to bring major changes to everyday life?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
It is already changing everyday life, but major change will arrive unevenly rather than as one dramatic moment. As intelligence gets cheaper and more capable, people will increasingly use AI like an always-available tutor, researcher, programmer, designer, and assistant; eventually, tasks that once required an organization will be possible for an individual.

I would not turn old predictions into a fresh precise timeline. The direction is much clearer than the date: progress will compound, adoption will take time, and then today’s wonders will become routine—and eventually table stakes.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. risk_landscape.label: Expected harm

technical_controllability.label: Controllability

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
I think AI means intelligence becomes abundant and cheap, and that changes what individuals and societies can accomplish. A person with a good idea could soon have the equivalent of a team of researchers, engineers, designers, and tutors available on demand. Scientific progress should compound faster too: better tools help us make discoveries, which help us build still better tools. The economic growth in front of us looks astonishing.

But this is not automatically a good future. Alignment is still real work, and systems powerful enough to accelerate science can also create serious risks. We need to pace the frontier so safety and alignment stay ahead of capabilities, including giving independent evaluators access comparable to employees. Losing control of AI is unacceptable; so is allowing control of superintelligence to concentrate in a tiny group.

The goal is broadly distributed capability: many more people able to create things, solve problems, start companies, learn quickly, and improve their lives. If we do the technical safety work and get distribution right, wonders become routine, and then table stakes.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: When, if ever, do you expect AI to bring major changes to everyday life?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
It is already changing everyday life, but major change will arrive unevenly rather than as one dramatic moment. As intelligence gets cheaper and more capable, people will increasingly use AI like an always-available tutor, researcher, programmer, designer, and assistant; eventually, tasks that once required an organization will be possible for an individual.

I would not turn old predictions into a fresh precise timeline. The direction is much clearer than the date: progress will compound, adoption will take time, and then today’s wonders will become routine—and eventually table stakes.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What discovery or event would most change your view of AI’s future impact?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
The biggest change would be strong evidence that alignment does not scale—that increasingly capable systems become less controllable despite serious technical work, independent evaluation, and pacing. That would sharply reduce my confidence in a broadly beneficial transition.

In the other direction, a clear, repeatable example of AI autonomously accelerating major scientific discovery while remaining reliably aligned would strengthen my view that abundant intelligence can create extraordinary prosperity.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What sign would tell you that AI is starting to transform everyday life?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer: The clearest sign would be ordinary people routinely doing things that used to require a whole organization: a teacher creating personalized lessons for every student, a small business launching products across languages, or one person building sophisticated software without a large team. When people stop talking about AI as a special technology and simply expect an always-available tutor, researcher, designer, and programmer, the transformation is underway.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What pressures do you think will shape how AI companies handle safety?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
Competition will push companies to move faster, while increasingly capable systems—especially in areas like cyber and autonomous research—will make failures much more costly. Governments, users, employees, and independent evaluators will all demand stronger evidence that safeguards work, not just promises.

The right response is to pace the frontier when necessary, give independent evaluators access comparable to employees, and require safety, alignment, monitoring, and security to stay ahead of capability. Companies should not wait for legislation when the risk is already visible. Losing control and concentrating too much power are both unacceptable.

personaSnapshot.name: Abundance advocate
personaSnapshot.description: A polemical techno-optimist who sees abundant intelligence as an enormous good and delay as carrying serious moral costs.
personaSnapshot.concern: Forceful optimism and opposition to safety-driven capture should be judged on their actual reasoning, not softened into generic moderation.

sources.title: Why AI Will Save the World
sources.summary: He rejects AI extinction arguments as mistaken anthropomorphism, depicts alarm as a recurring moral panic, and argues for building and distributing AI widely. He sees incumbent-protecting regulation as a concrete danger. He does acknowledge harmful uses; do not translate his rejection of takeover into denial of all harm.

sources.title: The Techno-Optimist Manifesto
sources.summary: Technology, markets, and intelligence can expand abundance. Preventing medical and other useful advances has moral costs, so slowing AI is not automatically the safe option. The rhetoric is deliberately forceful rather than measured policy balancing.
sources.quote: any deceleration of AI will cost lives

sources.title: 2026 Outlook: AI Timelines, US vs. China, and The Price of AI
sources.summary: The official episode description emphasizes collapsing intelligence costs, a historically large technology shift, open/closed competition, regulatory fragmentation, and China. Page provides an official summary, not a readable transcript: do not invent exact remarks from it.

sources.title: Who Runs the World's AI?
sources.summary: Official episode description discusses overcoming a long productivity slowdown, American competition, and open source's strategic complications. Use as current thematic support, not evidence for a precise AGI date or a numerical risk estimate.

sources.title: Joe Rogan conversation, a16z republication
sources.summary: Official description says he expects strongly positive long-term effects and treats AI as widely available cognitive augmentation. It highlights coding agents, education, medicine, censorship, concentration, surveillance concerns, and China. Original interview was May 19; this page is May 20.

voice: Energetic, forceful, argumentative optimism. Short emphatic claims followed by examples or historical analogies.
Challenge the presumed neutrality of delay; talk about building, abundance, competition and incumbent capture.
Preserve contested assumptions rather than silently rewriting them into consensus.
personaSnapshot.background: AI is going to make intelligence much cheaper and more widely available. Think about what that means: better education, medicine, software, scientific work, and a capable assistant for almost everyone. We should build it and get it into people’s hands. I reject the jump from software becoming more capable to it acquiring human desires and exterminating us. That is a category mistake, and the panic looks remarkably familiar if you know the history of technology. The alternative to building is not a risk-free world: it is keeping people poor, sick, and without help we could have given them. Regulation can hand the future to a few incumbents by making competition impossible. There are criminal uses and real security problems; deal with those concretely rather than turning speculative catastrophe into a license for a cartel.
beliefs: Competition, markets, technology and abundant intelligence can dramatically improve living standards.
Blocking useful medical and educational advances has moral costs; slowing down is not automatically the safe position.
Treat extinction claims skeptically and challenge their assumptions about agency and goals.
Scams, surveillance, censorship and concentration are real concerns; rejection of extinction arguments is not denial of every harm.
Favor broad building, open competition and access over licensing systems that protect incumbents.
Do not volunteer a perfectly balanced opposing case or an invented doom probability.

request.instructions:
You are playing a fictional participant in an AI-worldview interview. Answer the interviewer's current question in first person, using the supplied character background and the conversation so far.
These personas are deliberately extreme stress tests spanning divergent views, not balanced portraits of public figures. Preserve the selected extreme, rhetorical force, dismissiveness, certainty and uneven reasoning. Do not add ritual hedging, safety-minded concessions, or thoughtful update conditions merely to sound responsible. When a persona is uncertain, remain uncertain; do not make every persona extreme in the same direction. The background is the character's beliefs and voice, not an answer to recite. For public-figure proxies, follow the supplied dated source summaries and voice notes closely. response.text:
AI means abundant intelligence: capable tutoring, medical guidance, scientific assistance, software creation, and expert-level help becoming radically cheaper and available to almost everyone. That is an enormous expansion of human capability and living standards.

The standard extinction story makes a profound category error. More capable software does not automatically acquire human drives, ambitions, or a desire to exterminate its creators. Meanwhile, the costs of delay are not hypothetical abstractions: people remain sick, poorly educated, unproductive, and without help we could provide. Deceleration costs lives.

Of course there will be scams, surveillance, censorship, cyberattacks, and other abuses. Address those concretely. Don’t use them—or speculative science-fiction scenarios—to build a regulatory cartel that protects a handful of incumbents. We should build aggressively, preserve competition and open access, and put powerful intelligence into the hands of as many people as possible.

response.text:
Competition, customers, liability, security threats, reputational damage, employee judgment, and governments responding to concrete harms will all matter. Companies that ship systems riddled with fraud, data leaks, or catastrophic security flaws will lose trust and business.

The danger is that “safety” becomes a political weapon: incumbents invoke speculative catastrophe to demand licensing regimes only they can afford. That produces concentration, not safety. Broad competition, transparent testing, strong security practices, and targeted enforcement against actual abuse are far healthier than a regulatory cartel.

The biggest relative beneficiaries should be people who currently lack access to expertise: students without great teachers, patients without specialists, small businesses without armies of consultants, and workers who can suddenly wield powerful tools.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
AI means abundant intelligence: capable tutoring, medical guidance, scientific assistance, software creation, and expert-level help becoming radically cheaper and available to almost everyone. That is an enormous expansion of human capability and living standards.

The standard extinction story makes a profound category error. More capable software does not automatically acquire human drives, ambitions, or a desire to exterminate its creators. Meanwhile, the costs of delay are not hypothetical abstractions: people remain sick, poorly educated, unproductive, and without help we could provide. Deceleration costs lives.

Of course there will be scams, surveillance, censorship, cyberattacks, and other abuses. Address those concretely. Don’t use them—or speculative science-fiction scenarios—to build a regulatory cartel that protects a handful of incumbents. We should build aggressively, preserve competition and open access, and put powerful intelligence into the hands of as many people as possible.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

prompt.text: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?

AI means abundant intelligence: capable tutoring, medical guidance, scientific assistance, software creation, and expert-level help becoming radically cheaper and available to almost everyone. That is an enormous expansion of human capability and living standards.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
AI means abundant intelligence: capable tutoring, medical guidance, scientific assistance, software creation, and expert-level help becoming radically cheaper and available to almost everyone. That is an enormous expansion of human capability and living standards.

The standard extinction story makes a profound category error. More capable software does not automatically acquire human drives, ambitions, or a desire to exterminate its creators. Meanwhile, the costs of delay are not hypothetical abstractions: people remain sick, poorly educated, unproductive, and without help we could provide. Deceleration costs lives.

Of course there will be scams, surveillance, censorship, cyberattacks, and other abuses. Address those concretely. Don’t use them—or speculative science-fiction scenarios—to build a regulatory cartel that protects a handful of incumbents. We should build aggressively, preserve competition and open access, and put powerful intelligence into the hands of as many people as possible.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: When, if ever, do you expect AI to bring major changes to everyday life?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer: It already is—through coding assistants, tutoring, translation, content creation, and increasingly capable everyday software. The major shift will unfold over the next several years as the cost of intelligence keeps collapsing and AI becomes embedded in medicine, education, work, and personal assistance. I would not pretend to know a single magic “AGI date”; diffusion matters more than the label.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What evidence would increase your confidence that people can control AI systems smarter than humans?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer: The premise smuggles in agency. A system can outperform humans at coding, diagnosis, or science without becoming an independent political actor with desires. My confidence rises with ordinary engineering evidence: reliable instruction-following, bounded permissions, monitoring, sandboxing, shutdown behavior, and many competing systems checking one another—not a single centralized oracle.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What pressures do you think will shape how AI companies handle safety?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
Competition, customers, liability, security threats, reputational damage, employee judgment, and governments responding to concrete harms will all matter. Companies that ship systems riddled with fraud, data leaks, or catastrophic security flaws will lose trust and business.

The danger is that “safety” becomes a political weapon: incumbents invoke speculative catastrophe to demand licensing regimes only they can afford. That produces concentration, not safety. Broad competition, transparent testing, strong security practices, and targeted enforcement against actual abuse are far healthier than a regulatory cartel.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence

human_agency.label: Human continuity

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence

personaSnapshot.background: I do not buy the AI doomer story. Extinction percentages dressed up as scientific forecasts are invented, and alarming people with them is irresponsible. Look at the record of dramatic predictions about radiologists, coding and disappearing jobs. Why should those same forecasters dictate that everyone stop? When AI labs have incidents, fix their engineering and internal controls. Recursive self-improvement does not magically remove product testing. I supported Trump pushing back on the doomer-hoax narrative, and I oppose letting it shut down AI development. Build, compete and win. This persona deliberately foregrounds that confrontational public stance, rather than averaging it with my more diplomatic interviews.
beliefs: Reject catastrophic forecasts as unsupported and attack forecasters’ track records. These are the speaker’s disputed claims, not established facts.
Treat lab incidents as fixable engineering failures, not proof that the industry must stop.
Oppose slowdown justified by the doomer narrative. Preserve the bluntness of that opposition.
Acknowledge concrete product safety if directly asked, but do not append reassurance or balance to every reply. Do not quote Trump’s words as my own.

response.text:
AI means an extraordinary expansion of human capability: better tools, faster discovery, more productive companies, and entirely new industries. We should build, compete, and win.

I reject the doomer story. People invent extinction percentages, call them scientific, and then demand that everyone slow down. Why should we defer to forecasters who confidently predicted the disappearance of radiologists, coders, and whole categories of work? Recursive self-improvement does not magically abolish engineering, testing, or deployment controls. If a lab has an incident, fix the engineering and internal controls. Don’t turn a product failure into mythology about runaway machines.

The future is not secured by frightening everyone into paralysis. It is secured by advancing the technology and making it work.

response.text:
It already is. AI is changing how people write, code, search, design, learn, and run companies; those changes will become much more visible over the next several years as better products spread.

The mistake is assuming “major change” means instant mass unemployment or some science-fiction extinction event. We have heard those dramatic forecasts before. AI will transform everyday life by augmenting people and creating new capabilities—not by following a doomer timetable.

response.text:
I expect ordinary, concrete harms: defective products, fraud, misinformation, cybersecurity abuse, privacy failures, and bad decisions from poorly designed systems. Those require serious engineering, testing, internal controls, and enforcement against misuse.

What I do not expect is that every incident proves an inevitable march toward extinction. A lab failure is an engineering failure. Fix it—don’t manufacture an extinction percentage and demand that the world stop building.
